title: Lecture 17 – Ocular trauma
html:
Source: c17 trauma.pptx – 29 slides

Traumatisms of the ocular adnexa and the eyeball #1

(1) microtraumatisms of the conjunctiva and cornea; #2

  • (2) blunt injuries;
  • (3) penetrating injuries,
  • (4) burns

Microtraumatisms of the cornea and conjunctiva #3

  • foreign bodies on the cornea or under upper eyelid
  • Symptoms and signs
  • blinking and watering
  • foreign body sensation
  • “something existing within the eye”,
  • piece of grit, stone or sand under the upper lid

Microtraumatisms of the cornea and conjunctiva #4

  • Treatment
  • the upper eyelid has to be everted
  • foreign body removal (topic anesthesia)
  • antibiotics and astringents drops topically

Blunt injuries #5

  • contusions or concussions of the ocular adnexa or the eyeball

Eyelids #6

  • ecchymoses; bruises; excoriations;
  • lacerations;
  • superificial wounds

Conjunctiva #7

  • subhconjunctival hemorrhages
  • immediately after trauma, absorbing normally within 7-10 days
  • if bilateral (1-2 days after a cranial trauma).
  • a clinical sign, (sometimes the lonely one)of fracture of the cranial base.

Orbit #8

  • during the craniofacial contusions
  • fractures of the orbital walls and/or the walls of the orbit canal

Sclera #9

  • scleral rips
  • zones of minimal scleral resistance :
  • the equator area where sclera is thinner
  • the area next to corneoscleral limbus where anterior ciliary arteries enter the eye globe, reducing scleral resistance
  • the iris, ciliary body or even the lens may be incarcerated under the conjunctiva.

Cornea #10

  • erosions or abrasions
  • profound keratitis with edematous and cellular infiltration of the parenchyma and folds of the Descemet’s membrane

Anterior chamber #11

  • hyphema
  • bleeding that deposits in the inferior part of the anterior chamber as a horizontal level
  • Can lead to secondary glaucoma

Iris #12

  • radial rips of the pupillary margin with stiffness of the pupil
  • iridodyalisis
  • a detachment of the iris root from the ciliarty body

Lens #13

  • subluxation;
  • Luxation
  • anterior chamber
  • vitreous
  • subconjunctival
  • cataract

Ocular fundus #14

  • choroidal rips
  • usually located in the macula
  • edema of the retina
  • associated or not with hemorrhages
  • tears of the retina
  • retinal detachment
  • especially in persons with predisposing conditions
  • myopic eyes and eyes
  • arteriosclerotic changes

Treatment #15

  • symptomatic
  • lubricants antibiotics midriatics topically
  • surgery is mandatory
  • scleral rips, iridodyalisis,
  • subluxation and luxation of the lens

Penetrating injuries #16

  • ocular adnexa or the eyeball

Eyelids #17

  • eyelid wounds
  • if parallel with the free margin of the eyelid they tend to spontaneously heal due to contraction of the orbicular muscle
  • should involve the free margin of the eyelid,
  • surgery for restoring the continuity of the eyelid margin.

Orbit #18

  • may involve
  • optic nerve (vision disturbances)
  • extraocular muscles (strabismus,)
  • orbital vessels (hemorrhages)
  • foreign body may be retained within the orbit

Cornea #19

  • ocular hypotony
  • prolapse of the iris, lens capsule or vitreous
  • the pupil is distorted in shape
  • elongated towards the site of the prolapse
  • Sclera
  • without ocular hypotony

Complicatons #20

  • exogenous infection
  • exogenous septical uveitis that may evolve towards panophthalmitis
  • intraocular retention of the foreign bodies
  • Improper reconstruction of the AC may lead to adhesions between the iris and the angle ,
  • secondary angle closure glaucoma.
  • retinal injury at the site of the impact can lead to retinal detachment.

Intraocular foreign body #21

  • iron foreign bodies
  • ocular siderosis,
  • damage to the receptors and may manifest itself years later.
  • Copper foreign bodies inflammatory ocular chalcosis)
  • uveitis and hypopyon phthisis bulbi
  • Organic foreign bodies (wood)
  • endophthalmitis

Treatment #22

  • surgery
  • eyelid wounds,
  • extraocular muscle lesions,
  • corneal and scleral penetrating wounds,
  • intraocular foreign bodies.

Burns #23

  • Etiology
  • eyelids, conjunctiva, cornea, and the sclera
  • physical burns
  • high temperature (flame, electrical spark, electric current of high tension, inflammable liquids, hot liquids, incandescent metals)
  • ultraviolet radiations (phototraumatisms)
  • chemical burns
  • acid and alkaline substances.

Sign and symptoms #24

  • First degree
  • hyperemia of both the eyelid skin and the conjunctiva
  • corneal erosions without modification of its transparency
  • heal usually rapidly without sequelae
  • Second degree
  • phlyctenules of the eyelid skin
  • conjunctival erosions
  • a hyperemic and chemotic conjunctival background
  • corneal erosions or corneal ulcerations
  • mild diminishing the corneal transparency (cloudy cornea)
  • exogenous toxical anterior uveitis

Sign and symptoms #25

  • Third degree
  • profound necrotic lesions of the eyelids;
  • conjunctiva is pale and necrotic with erosion
  • cornea is ulcerated and opaque
  • sclera may present deep necrotic damages
  • early or late perforation of the cornea and sclera may follow
  • exogenous uveitis (always present)

Sign and symptoms #26

  • complication
  • eyelid retractions (ectropion and sometimes lagophthalmos)
  • adherent scars
  • between bulbar and palpebral conjunctivae (symplepharon)
  • expand sometimes upon the cornea (ankyloblepharon)
  • vascularized corneal leucomas (loss of the sight)

Pathophysiology #27

  • physical burns
  • cause the tissue albumins to coagulate arresting in this way spreading the lesions.
  • chemical burns
  • acid substances
  • coagulation of tissue proteins so their action is neutralized ceasing in this way their corrosive effect
  • alkaline substances
  • liquefaction of the tissue albumins allowing their caustic action to carry on within the next days after accident.

Treatment #28

  • no attempt for a specific antidote of acid and alkaline substances;
  • copious irrigation (large quantities)
  • warm water or saline solution
  • Midriatics topically
  • for preventing or treating the anterior uveitis
  • lubricants drops
  • antibiotics, antiseptics and topically dispensed

Treatment #29

  • ocular dressing
  • mechanical separation of the conjunctival surfaces (bulbar and tarsal conjunctivae)
  • glass rod or contact lens
  • to prevent from symplepharon formation
  • surgery
  • late complications
  • symplepharon, cataract, glaucoma.
